title: Seat a motor shield on a controller board without bending a pin
instruction: Press the motor shield down onto the controller board until it is fully seated, without bending its pins, then let go.
context: Stacking a motor driver on a controller board is a step of building and repairing small robots, and of the many hobby and teaching robots built on such boards. The shield's 32 pins have to go into the controller's sockets together: the contacts resist with about 50 N in all, so the shield must be pressed hard and evenly over the middle of its pins. Pressed at one end or on one row it tilts, the pins that are already in are levered over and bend, and the shield is scrap. A robot that can do this can take part in building and servicing robot controllers.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x away from the arms, y to the left); heights over the bench top. One fixed layout, nothing varies by seed. A carrier plate 100 x 80 x 6 mm, fixed to the bench, middle at x 28, y -20, long edges along x. On it an Arduino Uno R3 (68.6 x 53.3 mm, FR-4, four female header strips 8.5 mm tall at 2.54 mm pitch along its two long edges: 10 and 8 contacts on one edge, 8 and 6 on the other, the two rows 48.26 mm apart), screwed to the carrier on four 5 mm spacers, USB end towards the arms. An Arduino Motor Shield Rev3 (68.6 x 53.3 mm, about 25 g, 32 stacking-header pins 0.64 mm square under the board, its own sockets on top over the same four strips) rests on the Uno's sockets on its own pin tips, every tip 0.5 mm in its socket's lead-in, level, 5.5 mm above its seat; nothing else holds it. Nothing else is on the bench. Both arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: How far a header strip is in: how far its pin tips stand below the tops of the Uno's sockets (0.5 mm at the start, 6.0 mm seated). The score is the state at the end of the trial. 0: a pin has bent at any time in the trial (one strip 1.5 mm or more in while another stands 2.0 mm or more higher), or nothing below. 0.25: every strip 1.5 mm or more in. 0.5: every strip within 2 mm of its seat. 0.75: seated, every strip within 0.3 mm of its seat. 1.0: seated, the shield at rest and both grippers 3 cm or more from it; held for 1 s the trial ends as a success. Real bench: a ruler at the four corners for the 1.5 mm and 2 mm levels (the shield's board no more than 9.0 and 6.5 mm over the Uno's socket tops); a 0.3 mm feeler gauge between the pins' shoulders and the socket tops at the four corners for seated; the shield pulled off after the trial and its pins looked at for a bend; the video for the release.
reset_notes: Pull the shield straight off (about 44 N), check every pin against a straight edge and replace a shield with a bent pin, then set it back on the Uno's sockets with every pin tip in its lead-in and check that it stands level.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX; the boards are at true size from the maker's dimension drawing. The 32 spring contacts are not simulated: each of the four header strips meets one hidden seat that resists going down with 1.67 N for each of its pins (53.4 N in all) and stays where it was pushed. 1.67 N is the average insertion force of a 0.64 mm square pin in a Samtec SSW socket (data sheet F-215); the Uno's own sockets are unbranded, so the figure is assumed for them and is to be measured by pressing a shield onto an Uno that stands on a kitchen scale. The shield's place over the Uno is given, as the pins in their lead-ins give it; it can go down and tilt about both level axes, up to 7 degrees. A pin bends by rule (the 2.0 mm is assumed), not by a simulated bending pin. Pulling out is not modelled: nothing but its weight holds the seated shield. Assumed and to be measured on the bought parts: the shield's mass, the pins' 6 mm of mating length, the 5 mm spacers. Seated or not shows as about four pixels in the right wrist camera's picture and not at all in the top camera's; the press is felt through the arm more than seen.
